opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I've been thinking about a lot lately, and honestly my view has shifted quite a bit.

When I started working on interpretability, a lot of my motivation was almost aesthetic. I come from a physics background, and in physics you want to understand things. You don't just want a model that predicts well; you want to know *why* it works, what the underlying mechanism is. So for me, mechanistic interpretability was a way to bring that physicist's curiosity to neural networks. Can we open the black box and find the "laws" inside?

But once you take automated research seriously, the picture changes in a couple of ways.

The first is about who the interpretation is for. Traditionally, interpretability assumes a human is the consumer. We want explanations that fit in our heads: a circuit with a few nodes, a symbolic formula, a clean picture. That's partly why I worked on things like KANs, because I wanted networks whose learned functions you could actually read off and maybe turn into symbolic formulas. If AI systems start doing a meaningful share of research themselves, though, the bottleneck may not be human understanding anymore. Maybe the AI doesn't need a human-readable explanation to make progress. That's a bit humbling, because it suggests some of what we called "understanding" was really about our own cognitive limits.

The second shift goes the other way, and I think it's actually more important. If AI is doing research, then interpretability becomes *more* necessary, not less, but for a different reason. It's no longer mainly about satisfying curiosity. It's about trust and verification. If an automated system proposes a new physical law or a new algorithm, how do we know it's real and not some artifact of overfitting or a shortcut? We need tools to check what the system is actually doing internally. So interpretability moves from being a kind of science of AI to being infrastructure for AI-driven science.

And there's a third, more optimistic angle: automated research could help interpretability itself. Interpretability has always been extremely labor-intensive. You stare at activations, you form hypotheses, you run ablations, and it takes months to understand one small circuit. That doesn't scale to frontier models. If AI agents can do that hypothesis-and-test loop for us, we might finally get interpretability at the scale it needs to be useful. In a sense, interpretability is a very natural first target for automated research, because the experiments are cheap and fully in silico.

So where I've landed is this: I care less about whether every explanation is beautiful to a human, and more about whether we can build a reliable bridge between what the machine knows and what we can verify. I still have the physicist's taste for simple, elegant structure, and I think that structure often exists and is worth finding. But I now see interpretability less as an end in itself and more as part of a larger question: how do humans stay meaningfully in the loop when machines are increasingly the ones doing the discovering?

r001.rationale: The response describes mechanistic interpretability as a way to understand neural networks and as infrastructure for AI-driven science, but does not call it the biology of AI.

r002.rationale: It discusses interpretability’s labor-intensive research process, but does not attribute an earlier centuries-long expectation to the inability to automate that research.

r003.rationale: It says automated research could help scale interpretability, but gives no prediction that this would make distant goals attainable within three to five years.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it has changed it quite a lot, and in two directions at once.

The first is a kind of humility. For a long time I thought of mechanistic interpretability as this very craft-like thing. You stare at a small model, you find a circuit, you name it, you write a nice paper with pretty figures. It felt a bit like being a naturalist in the nineteenth century, collecting specimens one by one. And I enjoyed that. But when I started seeing agents that could run the full loop themselves, propose a hypothesis about a neuron or a feature, write the probing code, run the ablation, look at the result, and revise, I had this slightly uncomfortable realization that most of what I was doing with my hands could be done by a system at a scale I simply cannot match. A human can study maybe a few hundred features carefully in a career. A model can look at millions overnight. So the "artisanal" version of the field, the part that was really about one person's intuition applied to one circuit, I think that part is going away, and I had to accept that.

The second direction is more optimistic, and it is really why I still care. If the cheap part becomes automated, then the question of what is actually worth understanding becomes the whole game. Automated research is very good at answering questions, but it is not obviously good at asking the right ones, or at knowing what counts as an explanation versus a description. You can have a system that produces ten thousand "this feature fires on X" statements, and you are no closer to understanding anything, because there is no theory tying them together. So my view shifted from "let's find more circuits" to "what are the organizing principles, the laws, that make all these circuits make sense." That is the physicist in me talking. I want the periodic table, not the list of elements.

There is also a strange recursive flavor to it that I find fascinating and a little unnerving. We are going to use models to interpret models. And then the interpretation itself is something you would want to interpret. So interpretability stops being a static picture of a frozen network and becomes more like a verification problem, or almost an epistemology problem. How do you trust an explanation produced by a system whose own reasoning you do not fully understand? I think that forces the field to become more rigorous, more mathematical, more about what counts as evidence, rather than about clever visualizations.

So if I had to summarize: automated research made me less attached to doing interpretability by hand, and much more attached to figuring out what the deep structure is that any interpreter, human or machine, should be looking for. In a way it made the field feel less like a hobby and more like a science.

r001.rationale: The response compares hands-on interpretability to nineteenth-century naturalism, but does not characterize mechanistic interpretability as the biology of AI.

r002.rationale: It describes a craft-like earlier view and says automated research changed that view, but does not attribute an expectation of centuries to the inability to automate research.

r003.rationale: The response gives no prediction that automated research could make interpretability attainable within three to five years.

astra-6.text:
I think it changes what we should aim for. If research becomes increasingly automated, mechanistic interpretability could become part of the research process itself: a system runs an experiment, examines what a model learned, forms a hypothesis, and then designs the next experiment.

But that also makes me care more about what counts as an explanation. It’s easy to imagine automating the production of plausible stories about neurons or circuits. The harder question is whether those explanations let you predict behavior or change it in a controlled way. Can you intervene on the mechanism and get the result you expected?

So I would put more emphasis on that loop between explanation and experiment. Automation could let us explore many more hypotheses, but we still need a way to distinguish a useful scientific understanding from a convincing description.

sol-6.1.text:
It has made me more interested in whether mechanistic interpretability can become a tool for discovery. Understanding what a model is doing is valuable, but I also want to ask: has it learned something that we don’t know, and can we extract that knowledge in a form we can use?

If we increasingly automate research, that question becomes very important. A model might find a useful pattern or make an accurate prediction, but we still want to turn that into an explanation, a hypothesis, or a principle that a scientist can test. Interpretability could help bridge that gap.

And there’s a feedback loop: AI can help us do interpretability research, and better interpretability can help us understand AI-generated discoveries. But we have to be careful that an explanation is actually faithful to the model. A convincing story isn’t enough; ideally, it should lead to predictions we can check.
